# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is an established, life-saving therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death. Improved survival with an implanted defibrillator was demonstrated in patients with coronary disease at high risk for ventricular arrhythmia in the landmark Multicenter Automatic Defibrillator Implantation Trial [1], and subsequent trials confirmed survival benefit across primary and secondary prevention populations [2]. However, conventional transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs) carry a well-recognised liability. At 10 years post-implant, the risk of lead failure can be as high as 25% in patients with a transvenous ICD [3]. Transvenous systems are susceptible to several short- and long-term complications including cardiac perforation and pneumothorax, lead dislodgement, venous obstruction, and infection [4].

The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was conceived to circumvent these intravascular hazards. In an effort to minimise lead complications, a totally subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator system was developed to avoid the need for transvenous lead placement [5].

## Early development and first clinical experience

The pivotal proof-of-concept work was published in 2010. Bardy and colleagues tested four different subcutaneous ICD configurations in 78 patients, ultimately settling on a parasternal electrode and a left lateral thoracic pulse generator configuration, then tested that configuration in 49 patients and established that the device was as capable as a traditional transvenous device of achieving defibrillation, though it required a greater energy expenditure [6]. To achieve reliable performance, design trade-offs were necessary: to achieve reliable defibrillation and arrhythmia discrimination, the device delivers only high-energy shocks (80 J), and the time to therapy is typically about 20 seconds [7].

Regulatory approval studies followed. The IDE study was the first large prospective trial of this system, designed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of the subcutaneous device [7]. Early registry experience reinforced these findings: the totally subcutaneous defibrillator was presented as a new alternative to the conventional transvenous ICD system to minimise intravascular lead complications [8]. Pooled analyses then consolidated the evidence base. In the IDE and EFFORTLESS studies, two large prospective studies reported 6-month to 1-year data on the first implantable defibrillator that avoids placing electrodes in or around the heart [9]. The full EFFORTLESS cohort confirmed durability: the registry demonstrated that the S-ICD fulfilled predefined endpoints for safety and efficacy, with midterm rates on complications, inappropriate shocks, and conversion efficacy comparable to rates observed in transvenous ICD studies [10], and these results were maintained through 5-year outcomes of EFFORTLESS registry patients with early generation devices [11].

## Randomised evidence: noninferiority and beyond

The decisive comparison came from the PRAETORIAN trial. Among patients with an indication for ICD therapy but not for pacing therapy, the subcutaneous ICD was noninferior to the transvenous ICD with respect to the cumulative incidence of the primary end point of device-related complications or inappropriate shocks [12]. ICD-related complications were seen in 15.1% of S-ICD patients versus 15.7% of TV-ICD patients after a median follow-up of 4 years, while lead complications occurred in 6.6% of TV-ICD patients compared with 1.4% of those with a subcutaneous device [13]. A secondary analysis confirmed that the S-ICD, developed to overcome lead-related complications and systemic infections inherent to TV-ICD therapy, was non-inferior with regard to the combined primary endpoint of inappropriate shocks and complications [14].

Long-term follow-up extended these observations. The PRAETORIAN-XL trial extended follow-up by an additional 4 years to investigate whether the S-ICD is superior to the TV-ICD with respect to device-related complications at 8-year follow-up, with the primary end point being the composite of all device-related complications [15]. Over that span there was no significant difference in the rate of all device-related complications, but rates of major and lead-related complications significantly favoured the subcutaneous device [16].

The single-arm UNTOUCHED study addressed the device in sicker patients. Designed to evaluate the inappropriate shock rate in a more typical, contemporary ICD population using standardised programming and enhanced discrimination algorithms, it demonstrated high efficacy and safety despite a relatively high comorbidity burden, with a 3.1% inappropriate shock rate at 1 year—the lowest reported for the S-ICD [17]. The ATLAS trial provided further randomised data in younger, higher-risk patients. There was a statistically significant reduction in perioperative lead-related complications, occurring in 1 patient (0.4%) with an S-ICD versus 12 (4.8%) with TV-ICD; the S-ICD reduced these complications without significantly compromising shock effectiveness, but with more early postoperative pain and a trend for more inappropriate shocks [18]. Contemporary registry data, including the S-ICD PAS real-world multicentre registry designed to assess long-term safety and efficacy in a diverse group of patients [19], support these findings.

## Limitations: patient selection, screening, and pacing

Several limitations shape patient selection. Unlike transvenous ICDs, subcutaneous ICDs currently do not provide ventricular pacing and are not uncommonly contraindicated at extremes of body size [20]. Because sensing is surface-based, careful pre-implant evaluation is essential. An electrocardiographic screening test was developed to identify patients at risk for T-wave oversensing; in one cohort, 8% of potential recipients failed the screening test [21]. T-wave oversensing is a key consequence of S-ICD programming, and eligibility is identified during a mandatory screening process in which surface ECGs in multiple postures are used as surrogates of S-ICD vectors, requiring at least one vector to pass in at least two postural positions [22]. Eligibility may be particularly limited in special populations: among patients with left ventricular assist devices, only 37.3% were found eligible for S-ICD implantation with both screening tests performed [23], and among ventricularly paced patients, only 16% remained eligible during exercise [24]. Refined algorithms have helped: a discrimination algorithm has been used to reduce inappropriate shocks with the subcutaneous ICD [25].

## Future directions

The principal remaining limitation is the absence of pacing. While the S-ICD has demonstrated safety and efficacy for malignant ventricular arrhythmias, a limitation lies in the inability to either pace-terminate ventricular tachycardia or provide prolonged bradycardia pacing support [26]. Two strategies address this. The first is a modular system. Paradigm-shifting technologies such as the S-ICD and leadless cardiac pacemakers have emerged to address lead-related complications, and the modular cardiac rhythm management system is the first to integrate wireless intrabody communication between devices to allow coordination of leadless pacing and defibrillator therapy [27]. The MODULAR ATP trial assesses a subcutaneous ICD in wireless communication with a leadless pacemaker capable of pace-terminating ventricular tachycardia [28], and the rate of communication success between the S-ICD and leadless pacemaker was 98.78%, with a complication-free rate of 97.2% [29]. The second is the extravascular ICD. The extravascular ICD has a single lead implanted substernally to enable pause-prevention pacing, antitachycardia pacing, and low-energy defibrillation, retaining the benefit of extravascular placement [30].

## Conclusion

Over fifteen years, the S-ICD has matured from a proof-of-concept device into a guideline-endorsed alternative to the transvenous ICD for patients without a pacing indication, supported by randomised noninferiority data, lower lead-related complication rates, and improving inappropriate-shock performance. Emerging modular and extravascular technologies promise to extend extravascular defibrillation to patients who also require pacing, potentially broadening the population that can benefit from a leadless or lead-sparing approach.
